relevance_reason: Original report identifying heterozygous GNAL mutations as the cause of autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia (DYT25), with clinical description of 8 families and functional BRET studies.

findings.statement: Fuchs et al. (2013) used exome sequencing in 2 families with autosomal dominant primary torsion dystonia (PTD) and found heterozygous mutations in the GNAL gene in both: a nonsense mutation (S293X) in family P, located within one of 3 regions of potential linkage (LOD scores 1.5 to 2.1), and a missense mutation (V137M) in family D1. Sanger sequencing of the GNAL coding region in 39 additional multiplex PTD families of mixed European origin who were negative for DYT1 and DYT6 mutations identified 6 additional novel mutations in 6 families (19%). Segregation with disease was confirmed in all families with DNA from multiple affected individuals, and none of the variants was found in dbSNP135, about 3,500 European exomes, or 572 control chromosomes.
quotes: Using exome sequencing in two families with PTD, we identified a new causative gene, GNAL, with a nonsense mutation encoding p.Ser293* resulting in a premature stop codon in one family and a missense mutation encoding p.Val137Met in the other.

To confirm GNAL as a causative gene for dystonia, we performed Sanger sequencing of the entire coding region in 39 additional multiplex PTD families of mixed European origin who were mutation negative for DYT1 and DYT6. We detected novel mutations in the GNAL gene in six additional families (19%)

None of the variants were detected in dbSNP135, ~3,500 European exomes or 572 control chromosomes that we tested. Segregation analyses confirmed transmission of the GNAL mutations with the disease phenotype in all families for which DNA from multiple affected individuals was available

findings.statement: Fuchs et al. (2013) described 28 individuals with definite dystonia from 8 multiplex families with GNAL mutations, all Caucasian of mixed European ancestry. Mean age at onset was 31.3 years (range, 7 to 54 years); onset was in the neck in 82%, and 93% had neck involvement at final examination, but most progressed to other sites and only 46% had focal dystonia at last examination. Cranial involvement was present in 57% and speech involvement in 44%; brachial onset was not observed and arm involvement occurred in only 32%, distinguishing the disorder from DYT6.
quotes: Among the 8 families with mutations there were 28 individuals with complete clinical information who had definite dystonia (Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1). Average age of dystonia onset in the carriers was 31.3, and ranged from 7–54 years.
Most carriers (82%) had onset in the neck, and 93% had neck involvement at final exam, however most progressed to have dystonia at other sites, and only 46% had focal dystonia at last exam.

Further, cranial involvement was present in 57% of carriers, and 44% had speech involvement. Brachial onset was not observed and eventual arm involvement was seen in only 32%, distinguishing GNAL from DYT6

findings.statement: Fuchs et al. (2013) summarized the phenotype in the 8 GNAL families as predominantly cervical dystonia with a relatively broad range of age at onset and spread to other muscles, especially facial muscles, in over half of subjects. Some individuals had generalized dystonia with leg onset, and other onset sites included larynx, jaw, and tongue.
quotes: The phenotype in the 8 multiplex families is predominantly one of cervical dystonia, with a relatively broad range in age onset and spread to other muscles, especially the facial muscles, in over one half of subjects.

findings.statement: In affected members of family P with primary torsion dystonia (previously reported; mixed Russian and Swiss Mennonite heritage), Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous c.878C>A nonsense mutation in the GNAL gene, resulting in a ser293-to-ter (S293X) substitution. The mutation was found by exome sequencing, co-segregated with dystonia in the family, and was not present in about 3,500 European exomes. In a BRET assay, the S293X mutant failed to support any D1R-driven responses.
quotes: Among these, the p.S293X variant in the GNAL gene co-segregated with dystonia in the remaining members of Fam P (Supplementary Fig. 1).
The p.S293X deletion mutant failed to support any D1R driven responses

findings.statement: In affected members of family D1 with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous c.409G>A missense mutation in the GNAL gene, resulting in a val137-to-met (V137M) substitution at a residue completely conserved in GNAL orthologs. The mutation was found by exome sequencing, segregated with disease, and was not found in 572 control chromosomes or about 3,500 European exomes. In BRET assays the mutant showed an intermediate phenotype largely consistent with impaired association with Gbeta-gamma subunits.
quotes: an additional variant in this gene, p.V137M, was found among the 20 missense variants shared by all 4 members in Fam D1; it segregated with the disease in this family (Supplementary Fig. 1) and was not observed in 572 control chromosomes we tested.
Two mutants found in dystonia patients, p.E155K and p.V137M, showed intermediate phenotypes largely consistent with impaired association with the Gβγ subunits (Fig. 2).

findings.statement: In 2 affected members of family S with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous c.463G>A missense mutation in the GNAL gene, resulting in a glu155-to-lys (E155K) substitution at a residue completely conserved in GNAL orthologs. In BRET assays, the mutant showed an intermediate phenotype largely consistent with impaired association with Gbeta-gamma subunits.
quotes: The p.V137 and p.E155 residues were completely conserved in GNAL orthologs (Fig. 1b).
Two mutants found in dystonia patients, p.E155K and p.V137M, showed intermediate phenotypes largely consistent with impaired association with the Gβγ subunits (Fig. 2).

findings.statement: In 4 affected members of family D2 with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous 1-bp insertion (c.283-284insT) in the GNAL gene, resulting in a frameshift and premature termination (S95fsX110), predicted to cause loss of function.
quotes: c.283-284insT | p.S95fsX110
We thus predicted that early truncating mutations would remove essential functional regions of Gαolf resulting in a loss-of-function phenotype (p.R21X, p.S95fsX110 and p.R198fsX210).

findings.statement: In 3 affected members of family H with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous 1-bp insertion (c.591-592insA) in the GNAL gene, resulting in a frameshift and premature termination (R198fsX210), predicted to cause loss of function.
quotes: We thus predicted that early truncating mutations would remove essential functional regions of Gαolf resulting in a loss-of-function phenotype (p.R21X, p.S95fsX110 and p.R198fsX210).

findings.statement: In 3 affected members of family T with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous c.61C>T nonsense mutation in the GNAL gene, resulting in an arg21-to-ter (R21X) substitution, which they predicted to be degraded by nonsense-mediated decay and produce no protein.
quotes: c.61C>T | p.R21X
In addition, p.R21X is likely degraded by nonsense mediated decay thus producing no protein.

findings.statement: In the proband of family N with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous 9-bp deletion (c.304-312delCCTCCAGTT) in the GNAL gene, resulting in an in-frame deletion of 3 amino acids (P102-V104del).
quotes: one in-frame deletion of 3 amino acids (p.P102-V104del)
c.304-312delCCTCCAGTT | p.P102-V104del

findings.statement: In 2 affected members of family B with primary torsion dystonia, Fuchs et al. (2013) identified a heterozygous possible splice site mutation (c.274-5T>C; chr18:11,753,820, hg19) upstream of exon 4 of the GNAL gene. Bioinformatic analysis suggested the wildtype sequence was 10 times more likely than the mutant to be found near an acceptor splice site, but the effect could not be proven because GNAL expression was undetectable in patient lymphoblasts.
quotes: one possible splice site mutation at position chr18:11,753,820 (hg19) (c.274-5T>C) upstream of exon 4 of GNAL

Bioinformatics analysis enumerating all possible splice sites in the human genome suggests that the wild type sequence is 10 times more likely to be found near an acceptor splice site than the mutant sequence.

However, we were unable to prove this hypothesis in patient samples, as lymphoblasts are the only tissue available, and GNAL expression is undetectable by semi-quantitative PCR and western blot analysis (data not shown).

findings.statement: Using a cell-based BRET assay in HEK293 cells in which Galpha-olf function is assessed by its interaction with Gbeta-gamma subunits during the D1 dopamine receptor-initiated cycle, Fuchs et al. (2013) found that the S293X mutant failed to support any D1R-driven responses, E155K and V137M showed intermediate impairment, and the control variant V16F behaved like wildtype. They concluded that the functional assay was suggestive of loss of function, and that GNAL mutations point to primary abnormalities of D1R and/or A2AR transmission in striatal neurons as possibly leading to dystonia.
quotes: The p.S293X deletion mutant failed to support any D1R driven responses while p.V16F, a variant found in a single control sample showed normal wild-type like behavior.
A functional assay testing several of the mutations is suggestive of a loss of function.
Identification of causative mutations in GNAL points to primary abnormalities of D1R and/or A2AR transmission as possibly leading to dystonia.

findings.statement: Fuchs et al. (2013) noted that dystonia was inherited in an autosomal dominant manner in the GNAL families. Because GNAL may be imprinted, they examined parental origin and found that dystonia was inherited equally from maternal and paternal sides, with no apparent phenotypic differences between maternally and paternally inherited cases.
quotes: Since dystonia is rare and inherited in an AD manner in these pedigrees, the causative mutation is expected to be an extremely rare heterozygous variant, shared by all affected family members.
Dystonia was inherited from maternal and paternal sides equally, and there were no apparent phenotypic differences between maternally and paternally inherited cases.

findings.statement: Fuchs et al. (2013) found no genotype/phenotype correlation with regard to mutation type, and phenotypes varied within families carrying the same GNAL mutation.
quotes: In addition, no genotype/phenotype correlation could be discerned with regard to mutation type and, as seen in Table 1 and Supplementary Table 1, phenotypes varied within families with the same mutation.

findings.statement: Fuchs et al. (2013) noted that GNAL is located on chromosome 18p, centromeric to the DYT7 and DYT15 loci, and that dystonia occurs in patients with 18p deletions, suggesting that absence of GNAL may contribute to dystonia in these cases.
quotes: GNAL is located on chromosome 18p centromeric to the DYT7 locus for focal dystonia and the DYT15 locus for myoclonus dystonia,. Dystonia occurs in patients with 18p deletions–, and absence of GNAL may be contributing to dystonia in these cases.

relevance_reason: Describes a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset, cervical-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia excluded from DYT1, which is relevant to adult-onset cervical dystonia loci such as DYT25.

findings.statement: Bressman et al. (1994) examined 53 individuals from 4 generations of a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia. Seven family members were affected, with a mean age at onset of 28.4 years (range, 7 to 50 years). In 6 of the 7, the neck was affected first; all 7 developed cervical dystonia, and 5 had dysarthria or dysphonia.
quotes: We examined 53 individuals from four generations of a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset ITD. There were seven affected family members, with a mean age at onset of 28.4 years (range, 7 to 50 years).
In six of the seven, the neck was affected first. All seven developed cervical dystonia, and dysarthria or dysphonia occurred in five.

findings.statement: Bressman et al. (1994) found that linkage data excluded the DYT1 region on chromosome 9q34 in this non-Jewish family with adult cervical-onset dystonia. They concluded that a gene other than DYT1 is responsible for some cases of adult cervical-onset dystonia.
quotes: Linkage data excluded the region containing the DYT1 locus, indicating that DYT1 was not responsible for ITD in this family.
This study provides evidence that a gene other than DYT1 is responsible for some cases of adult cervical-onset dystonia.
